# Introduction

## Background

Heart failure is a chronic condition in which the heart cannot pump enough blood to meet the body’s needs, reducing the flow of blood and oxygen to the body and vital organs. This occurs when the heart becomes weakened, stiff, or damaged [@cardiacbc]. The most common cause is damage to the heart muscle from a heart attack or from blocked arteries around the heart; other causes include high blood pressure, heart valve problems, and congenital heart disease [@cardiacbc]. Heart failure currently has no cure; instead, it is managed by monitoring symptoms and weight, limiting sodium and fluid intake, controlling blood pressure, and taking medication [@cardiacbc].

There is no single test that diagnoses heart failure; clinicians commonly rely on a combination of blood tests, echocardiograms, chest X-rays, and electrocardiograms [@cardiacbc]. One key measurement is the ejection fraction (EF), the percentage of blood the heart pumps out with each contraction. A normal EF is about 60%, and patients with an EF of 40% or lower are classified as having heart failure with reduced ejection fraction [@bcguidelines2023]. Blood tests also provide useful information: serum creatinine reflects how well the kidneys are working, serum sodium measures the sodium level in the blood, creatinine phosphokinase (CPK) is an enzyme released when muscle tissue is damaged, and anaemia indicates a low level of red blood cells or hemoglobin [@uci2020]. Previous studies using this data set found that age, kidney function, blood pressure, ejection fraction, and anaemia were significant risk factors for mortality [@ahmad2017], and that serum creatinine and ejection fraction alone could predict survival well [@chicco2020].

Heart failure is a significant health burden in British Columbia, where about 2% of the population, roughly 137,082 people, were living with diagnosed heart failure in 2020/21, with 18,512 new cases that year [@bcguidelines2023]. As the number of people living with heart failure grows, clinicians need ways to identify which diagnosed patients are at the greatest risk of death. A model that predicts mortality from routinely collected clinical measurements could help prioritize these patients for closer follow-up, faster optimization of guideline-directed medical therapy, and timely referral for advanced treatments. This matters because guideline-directed therapy can extend life by several years, but its benefits take months to appear as doses are gradually increased [@cardiacbc].

## Research Question

The purpose of this project is to answer the following question: can we predict whether a patient with heart failure will die during the follow-up period using their clinical characteristics (such as age, ejection fraction, serum creatinine, and serum sodium)? 

## Dataset Description

The data set used in this report is the Heart Failure Clinical Records data set from the UCI Machine Learning Repository [@uci2020], originally collected by @ahmad2017. It contains the medical records of 299 patients admitted to the Institute of Cardiology and Allied Hospital in Faisalabad, Pakistan, between April and December 2015. All patients were aged 40 or older, had left ventricular systolic dysfunction, and were classified as New York Heart Association (NYHA) class III or IV [@ahmad2017]. The NYHA classification grades heart failure severity from class I (no limitation of physical activity) to class IV (symptoms at rest), so classes III and IV represent patients with advanced disease [@aha_nyha]. 

Each row represents one patient. The available variables are age, anaemia, creatinine phosphokinase (CPK), diabetes, ejection fraction, high blood pressure, platelets, serum creatinine, serum sodium, sex, smoking status, and follow-up time. The target variable is whether the patient died during the follow-up period (death event), coded as 1 if the patient died and 0 otherwise. Follow-up time is excluded as a predictor because it is directly linked to the outcome: patients who died early necessarily have shorter follow-up times, so including it would leak information about the target. This question can be addressed with this data set because it contains a clearly defined binary outcome and clinical measurements that are routinely collected in practice. However, because the data come from 299 patients with advanced heart failure at a single hospital, the results may not generalize to patients with milder disease or to other populations.

# Methods

## Python Libraries Import
```{python}
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns
plot_color = "teal"
```


## Data Import and Preparation
```{python}
from pathlib import Path

# Define the dataset URL
url = "https://archive.ics.uci.edu/ml/machine-learning-databases/00519/heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv"

# Define the raw data directory
raw_dir = Path("../data/raw")

# Create the directory if it doesn't exist
raw_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Define the file path
raw_file = raw_dir / "heart_failure_clinical_records_dataset.csv"

# Download and save the raw dataset if it doesn't exist
if not raw_file.exists():
    df = pd.read_csv(url)
    df.to_csv(raw_file, index=False)
else:
    df = pd.read_csv(raw_file)

df.head()
```


## Data Inspection
```{python}
row_ncol=df.shape

df_n_na=df.isna().sum()
duplicates=df.duplicated().sum()

print(f"The features/attributes of this dataframe are : {col_names}")

df.info()
```

## Inspect target Variable
```{python}
motaility_percentages=df["DEATH_EVENT"].value_counts(normalize=True)*100
print(round(motaility_percentages,1))

#Visualise the target distribution

sns.countplot(data=df, x="DEATH_EVENT")

plt.title("Distribution of Mortality Outcomes")
plt.xlabel("Death Event (0 = Survived, 1 = Died)")
plt.ylabel("Number of Patients")
plt.xticks([0, 1], ["Survived", "Died"])
plt.show()

```

Frome the visual above, the training data contains more patients who survived than died during the follow-up period. ~ 68% survived and 32% experienced a death event, indicating an imbalance in the target classes, with survival being the majority class. This is important for model evaluation because accuracy alone may not adequately capture how well the model identifies patients who died.

## Data Splitting
```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

X = df.drop(columns=["DEATH_EVENT", "time"])
y = df["DEATH_EVENT"]

X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X,
    y,
    test_size=0.2,
    stratify=y,
    random_state=522
)

train_df = X_train.copy()
train_df["DEATH_EVENT"] = y_train

print("Training set:", X_train.shape)
print("Testing set:", X_test.shape)

```

### Saving Processed Data

We save the stratified training and test splits separately, with `DEATH_EVENT` as the outcome and follow-up time excluded. Feature scaling is fitted within the model pipeline during training.

```{python}
processed_dir = raw_dir.parent / "processed"
processed_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

test_df = X_test.copy()
test_df["DEATH_EVENT"] = y_test

train_df.to_csv(processed_dir / "train.csv", index=False)
test_df.to_csv(processed_dir / "test.csv", index=False)
```

The median age of patients who died was slightly higher (approximately 62 years) than those who survived (60 years), and the patients who died also showed a wider age distribution. This suggests that older age may be associated with mortality in our dataset, although the overlap between the groups indicates that age alone may not distinguish mortality outcomes.

The mortality proportions are very similar between females (approximately 33%) and males (approximately 32%), suggesting that mortality rates do not differ substantially by sex in our training data. Despite males being more numerous in the dataset, the proportion of deaths within each sex is comparable, indicating that sex alone may have limited ability to distinguish mortality outcomes.

## Model Development

### Baseline Model

We first use a Dummy Classifier as a baseline to evaluate whether our classification model performs better than simply predicting the majority class.

```{python}
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier

dummy_model = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent")

dummy_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

dummy_pred = dummy_model.predict(X_test)
```


### Logistic Regression

We use logistic regression to predict mortality outcomes based on clinical measurements. StandardScaler is applied to standardize the features before model training.

```{python}
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

logistic_model = make_pipeline(
    StandardScaler(),
    LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000, random_state=522)
)

logistic_model.fit(X_train, y_train)

logistic_pred = logistic_model.predict(X_test)
```

## Model Evaluation
We evaluate the Dummy Classifier and Logistic Regression using stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training data. We compare accuracy, recall, and F1-score to assess their predictive performance.

- **Accuracy** measures the proportion of all predictions that are correct. It gives an overall comparison with the baseline, but the baseline can score reasonably well by always predicting survival because survivors are the majority.
- **Recall** measures the proportion of observed deaths that the model correctly identifies. Low recall means the model misses many patients who died during follow-up.
- **F1-score** is the harmonic mean of precision and recall for the death class. It rewards identifying more observed deaths while also accounting for false positives, which reduce precision.

```{python}
from sklearn.model_selection import StratifiedKFold, cross_validate
import pandas as pd

cv = StratifiedKFold(
    n_splits=5,
    shuffle=True,
    random_state=522
)

models = {
    "Dummy Classifier": dummy_model,
    "Logistic Regression": logistic_model
}

results = []

for name, model in models.items():
    scores = cross_validate(
        model,
        X_train,
        y_train,
        cv=cv,
        scoring=["accuracy", "recall", "f1"]
    )

    results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Accuracy": scores["test_accuracy"].mean(),
        "Recall": scores["test_recall"].mean(),
        "F1-score": scores["test_f1"].mean()
    })

results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

print(results_df.round(3).to_string(index=False))
```

### Final Test Evaluation

After comparing the models using cross-validation, we evaluate Logistic Regression on the held-out test set.

```{python}
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score, f1_score, confusion_matrix

test_pred = logistic_model.predict(X_test)

print("Test Accuracy:", round(accuracy_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))
print("Test Recall:", round(recall_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))
print("Test F1-score:", round(f1_score(y_test, test_pred), 3))

print("\nConfusion Matrix:")
print(confusion_matrix(y_test, test_pred))
```
# Results
### Classification Results

We compared a Dummy Classifier and Logistic Regression using stratified 5-fold cross-validation on the training set.

Logistic Regression achieved an average accuracy of 74.9%, recall of 44.4%, and F1-score of 0.530, outperforming the Dummy Classifier, which achieved 67.8% accuracy and zero recall and F1-score.

On the held-out test set, Logistic Regression achieved an accuracy of 73.3%, recall of 42.1%, and F1-score of 0.500.

The confusion matrix showed that the model correctly identified 8 of the 19 patients who experienced a death event, while 11 were incorrectly classified as not experiencing a death event.

These results suggest that clinical measurements provide useful predictive information. However, the relatively low recall indicates that the model has limited ability to identify patients who experienced a death event.
